displayTitle: 2026-07-29 - Social Services and Community Committee - Copyright (Parody and Satire) Amendment Bill
description: Wednesday, 29 July 2026 | Social Services and Community Committee Copyright (Parody and Satire) Amendment Bill Hearing of evidence: Miss Joanna McDonald Mr Tim Batt New Zealand Law Students' Association Jasmine McTavish, Education Vice-President Matthijs Siljee Professor Graeme Austin
descriptionSummary: Copyright (Parody and Satire) Amendment Bill. Miss Joanna McDonald. Mr Tim Batt

chunks.text: Mm-hmm.

Where were we up to? Item 14. 14. 14. Copyright. Yeah. Gotcha. Thank you. Just switch back from- Yeah... all the things you were just working on to Exactly. Sorry, I was on the wrong one. I was on the- No, it's all right. Yes, good to see you.

Joanna's on. Oh, she's online. Excellent. Joanna, I think just double check we've got you there. Yep. Apologies, I don't have a working web camera at the moment. Oh, no. Not a problem at all. We can hear and see you. So look, welcome to the Social Services and Community Select Committee this afternoon. We've got you for five minutes on the Copyright Bill. So, time is yours when you're ready to go.

Well, thank you to the committee for hearing me today. I am wanting to talk about this bill in two ways. Both that satire and parody have been a pillar of democracies, republics, a way for individuals and organizations to have their say on society and on their governance for millennia. Some of the earliest satire that we have is

in Roman texts and Aristophanes from 400 BC. So- Well, this is not something that needs to be looked at as, "Oh, shock, horror, people are making fun of people." This has happened forever, and I think this tradition should continue and be allowed to continue as freely as possible. Because if you can't criticize your government, if you can't make fun of those in power, then that just detracts from

the functioning of that government in some ways. The other thing that I would want to bring up in relation to this bill is, while it's a good bill, I like it, I would like to see greater clarity about who can operate under that bill. So, if individuals have rights under this bill in terms of satire and parody, or if businesses, where is the line between what is just fair use

and what becomes a commercially sensitive issue? So for instance, if I, in my business, was to do advertising that kind of makes folks fun at other competitors' advertising, similar to the famous Coke versus Pepsi advertisements overseas, where does the line get drawn? And it would be great to have greater clarification and opportunity for businesses and societies to basically state, "We are safe saying this. We're not going to be sued

or treated as libelous or anything because we are making a joke, because we are saying, 'Hey, you see this thing? Let's make light fun of it to be able to, as part of our advertising.'" So, there's been cases recently where not-for-profits supporting various communities have poked fun at other organizations that have been negative towards those communities

by just tweaking their branding and making light of their position. That should be allowed. You shouldn't be able to just be spreading utter falsehoods. But at the same time, there should be a degree to which, if I want to reference another organization or another business in a way that doesn't demean that other business

dramatically, while still poking fun at them, that should be totally fine. And that's also how advertising and business has been done for centuries. So, from a political standpoint, it's a tradition millennia old, and we should support reinforcing the ability to undertake that.

And from a business standpoint, it's also going to make things better for everyone. All right. If there's any questions. No, we don't have enough time, but thank you very much, Joanou, for coming and making a submission this afternoon. Thank you for your time, and please pass this bill.

Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. All right, our next submitter is Mr. Tim Batt, also via Zoom. Kia ora. Okay. All right. Yep, no, we can see and hear you. So, look, welcome to the committee, and we've got five minutes with you this afternoon. So the time is yours when you're ready.

Wonderful. Kia ora, everybody. My name's Tim Batt. Thanks for the time here on the committee. I'll be reading from prepared notes just so I can keep my thoughts in order. Bit of background on me. I've been performing stand-up comedy for close to 20 years. I've been both the co-chair of the New Zealand Comedy Guild and a director of the New Zealand Comedy Trust, which is the governance body that operates the New Zealand International Comedy Festival.

I've been making TV, radio, podcasts, and live shows for about a decade and a half now. I submitted in support of this bill because our country is absolutely brilliant at comedy, and I find it crazy that we're so out of step with basically every other country on Earth when it comes to protecting parody and satire in our Copyright Act. As you will likely already know, the USA has got a specific fair use clause in Section 107 of their Copyright Act, protecting parody.

The UK, Australia, Canada have a fair dealing for parody protections in their copyright laws. And even the European Union, under its EU InfoSoc directive, provides member nations with a parody protection legal framework for their copyright laws. What you might not be aware of, though, is the real-world effect for the lack of legal protection for parody and satire, the effect that it has in New Zealand, because it does have a very real effect.

The reason I found out that we have no, well, a real lack of free speech provisions in our copyright laws is when I was first writing for TV, for Jono and Ben, and was told by our producers that everyone in the entertainment industry is essentially winging it When it comes to parody of copyrighted entities like famous movie franchises and characters.

So we were given instructions to never go too far with jokes in that direction because legally we have no protection if it ever gets tested. Oh. Hopefully, I don't have to explain to you how insidious it is that in the comedy environment have a lack of legal protections any time we might reference a brand name, a well-known company, or a famous character.

TV producers, networks, and broadcasters in this country have had a history of being very broke, and that means that the threat of legal action means a lot of ideas that may even potentially be perceived to be in the neighborhood of brushing up against the Copyright Act will get shut down in pre-production.

This has happened, and I'd like to give you an example. I've had a lot of ideas shut down in the writers' rooms of TV shows over the years, but one particular one I want to highlight actually happened to two friends of mine, Joseph Moore and Laura Daniel, both of whom are incredibly talented. They work on "SNL UK" now, and they're actually editing a brand new TV show that just got filmed here in New Zealand at the moment. They perform as a comedy pop duo called Two Hearts.

Now, at the New Zealand Comedy Gala, which is a televised live event that kicks off the comedy festival each year, they performed a really brilliant parody song that was stylistically referencing Disney's "Moana." And I say stylistically referencing because they specifically went to pains to make sure that they complied with the existing and incredibly onerous copyright laws of New Zealand to make sure that they did not fall afoul of it. They did their due diligence to ensure that they did not infringe on Disney's rights under New Zealand's current laws in any

way. They performed the song, everyone in the room loved it, and then TVNZ's legal team, who by my estimation acted completely out of fear rather than any serious legal rationale, stopped the performance from getting broadcast on TV. Again, the work did not infringe on anyone's copyright, but our laws are so lacking in protection that our broadcasters are financially terrified of legal action from big rights holders, and they censor stuff anyway.

Not only did that brilliant work of comedy get prevented from being broadcast and it was withheld from the public, this also meant that Two Hearts didn't get paid for it because your payout gets based on how much of your performance gets televised. Mm. So I wanted to give you a real-world example of not just the direct lack of legal protection, but the chilling effect of our laws being so out of step with the rest of the world.

I will end it there, but I just can't emphasize enough my personal recommendation and advocacy for this bill's adoption. Thank you. Thank you, Tim. Appreciate that. Look, just a quick question from me. We heard, I think it was last week, from the organization that represents about 3,000 creatives in New Zealand, and just concerns they had about this bill.

I think they were broadly in support of the objective, but the operationalization of this bill, they had some serious concerns about it not protecting the creatives that they represent. Do you have any comments on that? No. I don't sort of have enough expertise to comment on that in the moment. Okay. No. Not a problem.
When's your next show, Tim? Tonight. Hey. Well, break a leg, as they say. Thank you. Thank you very much. Much appreciated. I got to- Thanks, folks... appreciate it. Thank you. Cheers.
Law Students Association online as well. Excellent.

All right. Good afternoon and welcome to the New Zealand Law Society Association. Jasmine? Thanks, Joseph. Thank you. Tena koutou katoa. My name is Jasmine McTavish, and I'm appearing on behalf of the New Zealand Law Students Association. We are the national representative body for all law students across Aotearoa.

We provide advocacy and a united voice on all matters that affect our legal students. As with Tim, I'm going to be reading off some notes that I quickly formulated upon being informed that it was only a five-minute speaking time. So NZLSA does- No, we've got you for 10, we've got you for 10 minutes. Okay, fantastic. Cool. Mm-hmm. So NZLSA does support the bill in principle, as set out in our submission, particularly in recommendation one.

We consider this to be an overdue modernization of our New Zealand copyright law. We understand that our current framework doesn't provide sufficient certainty for creators engaging in forms of expression that are increasingly common in our modern society. However, our position is that the bill is an important first step, but that it requires further refinement to ensure that it operates effectively in practice.

The reason that this bill matters to the people that we represent is that students are often at the forefront of new forms of creative expression, whether it's a law review parodying a popular song, a student publication that may be using satire to comment on current political issues, a young creator producing online content, or students that are regularly engaging with parody and satire as a way of communicating their beliefs, their ideas and their values.

And to the students that we represent, these aren't simply forms of entertainment. They're ways that we're able to participate in public debates, to engage with our political issues, and to help develop our legal students' creative skills. However, we've identified that students and emerging creators often do this without access to any kind of specialist legal advice or any resources that larger organizations may have available to them.

And this uncertainty is a problem that we believe this bill has the opportunity to address. As discussed in part five of our submission, the current law creates a chilling effect. Our current framework looks at the fair dealing concept, and this creates a relatively narrow idea compared with the jurisdictions of Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States as well.

Because there's currently no specific exception for parody or satire, creators that are making any kind of content need to try and fit their work within any kind of existing category, and that might be criticism or maybe review. And this does create a kind of uncertainty for our courts as well.

For our students, our independent artists, and our emerging creators, a copyright dispute can be something that's really costly and intimidating, and this might stop them from expressing their views because they don't have that access to any kind of legal advice or any kind of understanding of what it is that they may have in front of them if they are to be found to be breaching what this bill is proposing. And this is where the connection with the freedom of expression becomes really important.

So Section 14 of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act recognizes the importance of our freedom of expression. And we're not suggesting that copyright protections should be weakened or that creators should lose any kind of control over their works, but rather that there is a balancing and a maintenance of the appropriate balancing.

We believe that copyright should be protective and should protect creativity, but it shouldn't necessarily prevent others or any kind of form of legitimate creativity, any kind of criticism, or any kind of commentary. So NZLSA has identified several ways in which we believe that this bill could be strengthened. And the first would be being through clearer guidance around the definitions of parody, satire, and fairness.

Also, as outlined in recommendation two, we recommend that the bill provides a non-binding statutory guidance on the meaning of parody and satire. We know that these concepts are inherently contextual, but providing any kind of guidance would assist both the creators and copyright owners, and maybe more importantly, the courts in making Parliament's intention clearer.

Our concern is that without any kind of guidance, courts may face uncertainty or unnecessary uncertainty when determining whether any kind of particular work qualifies. When looking at recommendation three, we understand that the bill appropriately requires that the use must be fair, but it currently provides very limited guidance on what that fairness requires.

Therefore, we have recommended that a non-exhaustive fairness framework could be created drawing on some of the existing copyright principles, and some of those relevant factors that could be included could be the purpose of the use, whether the work is transformative, the nature of the original work, the amount of original work that's used, and the effect on the market value for the original works.

So the purpose of these factors isn't to create a rigid test as such. It's just to provide a practical framework that protects copyright owners while also allowing some kind of genuine parody and satire to operate. We also want to highlight recommendation five, which relates to the practical operation of this exception online.

Much of our parody and satire occurs through digital platforms, especially with the students that we represent. However, these online platforms often rely on an automated copyright enforcement system and standard terms of service, and this creates a risk that statutory rights created by Parliament could be undermined by practice and by private arrangements.

A creator may have a lawful exception under the legislation but still have their content removed because of a platform's broader protections. So we recommend that a potential protection against contextual override be created. The final issue that we want to highlight is in recommendation four, and that relates to Tikanga Māori and Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations or considerations.

We consider that this is an important opportunity for this bill to reflect the very unique legal context of Aotearoa. We understand that our traditional copyright frameworks have largely focused on individual ownership and our economic interests. However, as recognized by the Waitangi Tribunal and Wai 262, there can sometimes be a mismatch between these concepts and the collective nature of both our taonga and Mātauranga Māori. And this is really important because parody and satire often involve radical or criticism.

And where taonga Māori are involved, potential harm isn't usually economic. It might relate to mana, whakapapa, cultural authority, and the responsibilities of kaitiaki. And these considerations aren't always captured through our traditional copyright concepts that are focused on that market value.

So our recommendation here isn't to prohibit parody from involving any kind of Māori content, but rather to ensure that our courts are able to consider Tikanga Māori and Te Tiriti principles when it's relevant when assessing fairness. And going back to fairness, we know that it, again, is inherently contextual, especially here in Aotearoa. That context includes that unique constitutional environment.

Thank you for your time, and I welcome any questions. Oh, thank you, Jasmine. We have our first question from Maude. Thank you, Ms. Chair. Jasmine, thank you for your really well put together submission. I just have a question around recommendation three, and in particular, D and E, and just wonder if you can give some guidance about how that could be quantified.
I'm sorry, one moment.
Sorry, I'm just pulling this up now. Okay. Which page are you looking at there, Maude? It's on page eight. Page eight. Thanks.

Recommendation three, D and E, and how it could be quantified. Yes. I believe that when looking at the amount and substantiality of the part of works used, there needs to be a balance when looking at the market value of the original work, and then also probably weighing up the intentions behind the creator's use of that, and whether that balance justifies.

Thank you very much, Jasmine. I would love to ask you some more questions, but we are at time now. But look, I just want to thank you for making a very comprehensive written and oral submission. Thank you. Thank you. Thanks, Jasmine. Thank you. Right, our next submitter is...
Matthias. In person. Welcome, Matthias. Real person. So welcome, come forward and take a seat there in the middle if you like.

All right, welcome. We have five minutes with you this afternoon, so the time is ready. Okay. Kia ora, thank you so much for giving me the opportunity to talk to you. I can't say that I'm an expert in governance or in legal matters. I came to New Zealand, Aotearoa, in '94 to work on Te Papa Tongarewa, the national museum, on the design team.

I'm an industrial designer by trade, and I also lecture at Massey University. So rather than being in the regulatory space, I'm a maker of things. And so my submission is less about technicalities and more about contextual things as I experience them from my profession.

And I want to speak to two points in my submission. They are the benefits of dissent. But first, I would like to reflect on the intentions and the imperfections of intellectual property protection, specifically copyright. To me, both notions, dissent and where parody and satire are part of, and copyright seem to be sitting in a weird unlogical relation to each other, like apples and cows, and I'd like to split them up and share separate thoughts and concerns on each.

I understand intellectual property, specifically copyright, to refer to an author's exclusive right to benefit from the expressions of ideas. When it comes to expressions of ideas, we seem to overlook fundamental notions that have been widely understood before copyright even existed, and that is, in reality, ideas exist everywhere. They are there for everyone to receive, to hold, to do something with, to share.

And also another notion that ideas are complex, they are interconnected, they are never singular. Now, how did we end up with copyright? When Gutenberg and others introduced movable type in Europe, it accelerated the printing and the spreading of ideas and the expressions of ideas throughout Europe. Printers found that their expressions of ideas would be ripped off, and so we began to treat ideas as singular and as property. And while it is a clunky approach, it was deemed reasonable that somehow the IP legal frameworks could give that author or the inventor

a fair go to get a return on investment. But it is clunky. And, as with many things, that are simple or intended to be simple, absurdities will always follow with it. We won't go too much into that. But it promoted the evolution of visual and material culture in Europe, as diverse expressions of diverse societal values.

So that is a point that I find very important in how ideas are being protected. Now, the emergence of machine learning is leading to the circumvention of those protections. And there are only very few beneficiaries, and it is at the expense of most of us.

IP is being harvested and rehashed to the lowest common denominator. Earlier in the advent of public internet There was the promise of access, the promise of unlimited proliferation of diverse expressions of ideas. That was the big dream that was going to happen, and the opposite is happening.

Media expert Dr. Claire Robertson gives evidence that while there are exceptions, most people worldwide have begun to severely narrow and conform their areas of interest, their norms, and beliefs. That is the measured result of the introduction of the internet. Mm. There's pros and cons to everything.

Now, when we look at AI, that has only accelerated that very same diminishing effect. So unless there is political will, the 19th- and 20th-century-based IP laws seem toothless in the face of this at the expense of diversity, critical reflection, collective wisdom, and diversity as a fundament for democracy.

Can we please update our laws to protect this? That's my first point. Okay. Then about parody and satire. Parody and satire are important political activities. They are there to balance or to challenge what is overpowering. They are there to hold those who are in charge to account, to draw spectacular attention at times to critical voices when those in power, and their mates in the lobby, do not like the messenger.

McKinsey researchers say that it is an important factor in successful governance, is engaging with dissent. Dissent is useful. It should not be stifled by improprietary rules. To use copyright rules to stifle sincere dissent is anti-political. It opens the door to power abuse.

It happens in societies where democratic checks and balances have been removed. These are the places where people try to run away from fast. Just to conclude, when copyright laws exist to what we deem a reasonable chance, to give a reasonable chance to authors before getting ripped off, stick with that, and do it well, especially when current laws do not do enough to protect small, medium-sized entities, designers, artists, people of the public, just anyone.

And when the appropriating, the exploiting, and the misrepresenting of customary knowledge, I'm not digging into Y262 here- Mm. The person before me has done that beautifully. And it's done by the most wealthy organizations on the planet. We'll have to draw to a closing time. Yep.

We are well over time. I fully support the amendment to the Copyright Act. Thank you very much. Thank you for coming, making a submission this afternoon. Thank you. Thank you. We next have Professor Graham Austin, also in person. Welcome. Thank you. Graham, welcome. We have five minutes with you this afternoon.

Oh, great. Thank you for your written submission as well. Thank you very much to speak with you today. As you've seen from my written submission, I strongly support the bill. I think it's the poster child for a good defense for copyright law. A whole lot of things come together. It's consistent with the aims of copyright law and that parodies are new works of authorship, and we want to encourage creativity, and so it aligns with those basic aims. As other speakers have said, it's a free speech safety valve, that these are typically criticism, social commentary, taking the Mickey out of

things. These are good things in a free and democratic society. And for a parody to do its job, it has to take quite a lot of the underlying copyright work. Otherwise, the parody won't work. And so that's another reason why a defense is needed, and we can't rely on other parts of the Copyright Act. And as I explained in the written submissions, it also solves or goes some way to solving a market failure problem. The Copyright Act's very clear. It says in Section 14, copyright is a property right, and in a society like ours, we tend to

say that property owners have the right to decide what happens with their property, whether they license it to other people, whether they monetize it, and so on. It's their choice. The problem with parody is that most people don't like to be lampooned, and so we can't rely on the copyright owners to enter into a licensing market for parodies. So this is one of those rare opportunities or rare instances where it's good for the law to step in and give people a nudge towards allowing these parodies. And the final reason is, I think

it brings our laws into line with Australia, Canada, broadly with the United States, and with the EU. If you go back to the first reason and say this helps encourage the creation of new works, if our laws align with other countries, that takes away some of the transactional friction when people want to market their parodies into other markets.

We want people to have international distribution deals for their creative work, and that lowers the friction. I suspect a number of other submitters have said the bill as currently drafted is too narrow, and that it needs to extend to audiovisual works. And I put some suggestions in the written submissions.

It may be aimed at the officials to help people think through how that might be achieved in a neat way so that the bill that comes into select committee is broadly consistent with the bill that comes out of select committee. I want to talk about definitions because there has been some discussion about whether definitions of these concepts are required in the act. We heard that from Jasmine's submission just a moment ago.

I don't think that's a good idea. If we are starting A few years ago, maybe. But in the case law from other countries, the judges are very good at sorting out what is a parody, what is a satire. And our judges and the people who write guidance for creative workers can draw on that quite easily.

And it might muddy the waters if we try and do this, and also bring in some inconsistencies in our law, which could create some of that legal and transactional friction. So, I think that's not necessary. And also, we need to remember that this is fair dealing for the purposes of parody and satire. And so, that fairness question is really important. And overseas, judges are really good at asking what is really the basic question here, which is should this content be licensed or not?

And that's the basic question here. It's not so much does it fit into the category of parody or satire or, in the EU, pastiche, et cetera. So, I think avoiding definitions, too, is probably a good thing. My final point is about moral rights, and there was some discussion of moral rights. A really good discussion in the first reading of the bill.

In most mature legal systems, moral rights and parody live together quite happily, and that's also a product of having parody tightly defined, so that it's very clear that it's not the original author's work. It's actually the parodist doing that. And when that's clear, then it doesn't prejudice the honor and reputation of the underlying author.

So, I think that the existence of moral rights in our legislation is not a problem for the successions. In sum, I'm in favor of it. It's something that's discrete, and doesn't need to wait for the broader copyright reforms that have been announced by the government in the wake of the two free trade agreements.

Might I ask you a really very quick question on that, because we heard last week from the We Create Alliance, which represents, I think, 40 of New Zealand's creative industries and organizations representing 30,000 Kiwi creators, et cetera, their view was that although change was needed, they thought it should be through a comprehensive best practice policy development approach.

And a comprehensive review of the Copyright Act was important, and their concern of this would be, basically, in their words, an ad hoc approach to dealing with one discrete issue. Mm-hmm. Any comment on that? Go back to the point, I think that this sits alone and is needed, and the other kinds of reforms that have been announced, such as getting rid of the three strikes regime, the introduction of blocking orders, those kinds of things are not going to affect the parody and satire defense that's been proposed in this bill.

So, I think they're separate issues, looking at what has been announced by the government. Great. Well, thank you very much for coming- Thank you... and making submissions. I have to thank the rest of the commission as well. Thank you. Right, that concludes public submissions on this bill this afternoon. Is there anyone else?
